The Case for Anarchy: Why the United States Should Be Dissolved

In a world where men with guns can take your money, lock you in a cage, or kill you for violating arbitrary rules you never agreed to, it is not the absence of government we should fear—it is its presence. The United States federal government, like all states, is an institution built on coercion, maintained through violence, and perpetuated by myth. It is time to recognize this fundamental truth: no just society can be built on the initiation of force, and true freedom, prosperity, and harmony can only flourish in the absence of state authority. The dissolution of the U.S. federal government and its replacement with a stateless society based on voluntary cooperation is not only morally imperative but practically superior in every meaningful way.

I. The Immorality of State Coercion

At its core, the state is an institution of systematic violence. Consider taxation: if an individual were to approach you with a gun and demand a portion of your income, we would correctly identify this as armed robbery. Yet when the IRS does the same, it is called "civic duty." The only difference is the scale of the operation and the euphemisms used to justify it. All state laws, from the mundane to the drastic, are ultimately enforced at gunpoint. Resist a parking ticket too vigorously, and you may find yourself at the wrong end of a police officer’s firearm. Refuse to pay taxes, and men with guns will eventually come to take you away. This is not governance; it is extortion on a societal scale.

Proponents of the state often invoke the myth of the "social contract" to justify this coercion. Yet this contract is a fiction. No living American has ever signed the Constitution, and even if they had, no contract can morally bind future generations. The reality is that we are born into this system without consent, and our only "choice" is to obey or face violence. As Lysander Spooner wrote in No Treason: "The Constitution has no inherent authority or obligation. It has no authority or obligation at all, unless as a contract between man and man. And it does not so much as even purport to be such a contract. It purports, at most, to be only a contract between the people themselves—'We the people'—not a contract between themselves and anybody else." The state’s claim to legitimacy is as flimsy as a highwayman’s demand for your wallet, justified only by his superior firepower.

Even democracy, often held up as the pinnacle of political legitimacy, is nothing more than mob rule. As Benjamin Franklin warned, "Democracy is two wolves and a lamb voting on what to have for lunch." The will of the majority does not make coercion moral. If 51% of the population votes to enslave the other 49%, it does not sudden make slavery just. The state, whether democratic, authoritarian, or monarchical, is still, at its core, an institution that rules by force.

II. The Inevitability of Corruption

Power corrupts, and absolute power corrupts absolutely. The state, as the ultimate concentration of power in society, is therefore the ultimate corrupter. History is replete with examples of governments that began with noble intentions only to descend into tyranny. But the corruption is not merely a risk; it is an inherent feature of the state. When power is centralized, it attracts those who seek to wield it for their own gain. Politicians do not enter office to serve the public good; they enter to serve themselves, their donors, and their allies. The revolving door between government and corporate boardrooms is not a bug of the system but a feature.

Consider the military-industrial complex, where private corporations profit from perpetual war, or the pharmaceutical industry, which lobbies to maintain its government-granted monopolies. These are not aberrations but the natural consequences of a system where power is concentrated and unaccountable. The state does not regulate industry; industry regulates the state. Even well-intentioned regulations often serve to entrench existing power structures, as smaller competitors are priced out or crushed under the weight of compliance costs that large corporations can easily absorb.

Moreover, the state’s monopoly on certain services ensures inefficiency and stagnation. Public schools, postal services, and infrastructure projects are notorious for their waste and inefficiency, precisely because they lack the discipline of competition. The U.S. Postal Service loses billions annually, yet derives its revenue not from voluntary customers but from a legal monopoly on first-class mail. Public schools in many districts are failing, yet parents have little recourse but to pay for private education on top of their taxes. In a stateless society, all services would be subject to the pressures of the free market, leading to constant innovation and improvement.

And let us not forget the monopoly on violence. The state claims the exclusive right to use force within its territory, yet this monopoly does not prevent violence—it institutionalizes it. Police officers, who are supposed to "protect and serve," kill over 1,000 Americans every year, with near-zero accountability. The wars fought by the U.S. government have resulted in the deaths of millions of innocent people abroad, from Vietnam to Iraq to the ongoing drone strikes in the Middle East. No private actor could ever inflict such widespread and systematic harm; only the state, with its claimed monopoly on violence, can commit atrocities on such a scale and with such impunity.

III. The Superiority of Voluntary Cooperation

If the state is dissolved, how would society function? The answer lies in the power of voluntary cooperation. Every day, billions of transactions occur without the involvement of the state. When you buy a cup of coffee, you do so voluntarily, because both you and the seller expect to benefit from the exchange. This principle can and should extend to all aspects of society.

Defense Without the State

Defense is often cited as a service that only the state can provide. Yet there is no reason why private defense agencies (PDAs) could not emerge to protect individuals and communities. In fact, they already do: private security firms protect businesses, gated communities, and even entire neighborhoods, and they do so more effectively and accountably than government police, who enjoy qualified immunity and often face no consequences for their actions. In a stateless society, defense agencies would be subject to market pressures, and those that violated their customers’ rights would quickly go out of business.

Critics claim that PDAs would lead to constant warfare between competing agencies. But this ignores the economic incentives at play. War is expensive, and businesses exist to make profits, not to engage in costly conflicts. Just as McDonald’s and Burger King compete through better service and lower prices—not by bombing each other’s restaurants—PDAs would have every incentive to resolve disputes peacefully through arbitration. Historically, private law and defense have worked: medieval Iceland operated for over 300 years without a state, relying on private arbitration and voluntary associations for security and justice.

Law Without the State

Law, too, can be provided through private arbitration and polycentric legal systems. In a stateless society, individuals and communities would subscribe to the legal frameworks of their choice, with disputes resolved by neutral third parties. Those who refused to comply with arbitrators’ decisions could be ostracized—denied access to markets, trade, and social cooperation—until they made restitution. This system worked in medieval Iceland, where the Althing (a voluntary assembly) resolved disputes without a centralized state. It works today in international commerce, where businesses often prefer private arbitration over state courts because it is faster, cheaper, and more predictable.

Welfare Without the State

Welfare is another area where the state claims a monopoly, yet history shows that voluntary mutual aid is far more effective and compassionate. Before the rise of the welfare state, mutual aid societies flourished in America and Europe, providing unemployment benefits, healthcare, and funeral services to their members. Fraternal organizations like the Knights of Columbus and the Odd Fellows provided social safety nets without a single dollar of tax money. Charities, religious organizations, and community groups have always played a major role in assisting the less fortunate, and they would only expand their efforts in the absence of government interference.

Voluntary cooperation is not only more moral than state coercion; it is more efficient. Government welfare programs are notoriously bureaucratic and wasteful, with much of the funding diverted to administrators rather than those in need. In contrast, private charities have strong incentives to use donations effectively, as donors can take their money elsewhere if they dissatisfaction with results. Studies have shown that private charities deliver far more services per dollar than government programs.

Money Without the State

The state’s monopoly on money, enforced through legal tender laws, has led to chronic inflation, boom-and-bust cycles, and the erosion of savings. Under the current system, the Federal Reserve can create trillions of dollars out of thin air, devaluing the currency and impoverishing those on fixed incomes. In a stateless society, competing currencies would emerge, with individuals free to use whatever medium of exchange they preferred—whether gold, Bitcoin, or private banknotes. This would eliminate inflationary monetary policy and restore sound money, benefiting savers and workers alike.

IV. Historical and Contemporary Examples of Stateless Success

The idea of a stateless society is not mere fantasy; it has been realized, albeit briefly and imperfectly, throughout history.

Anarchist Catalonia (1936-1939)

During the Spanish Civil War, the region of Catalonia was controlled by anarchist collectives, who abolished capitalism (in the means of production), organized production through worker cooperatives, and provided social services through voluntary mutual aid. Despite being under siege from both fascist and communist forces, these collectives achieved remarkable levels of productivity and social harmony. Unemployment was virtually eliminated, and industrial output increased dramatically. As George Orwell, who fought with the anarchists in the POUM militia, observed: > "I had dropped more or less by chance into the only community of any size in Western Europe where political consciousness and disbelief in capitalism were more normal than their opposites."

Medieval Iceland (930-1262 AD)

For over 300 years, Iceland operated as a stateless society under the Althing, one of the world’s oldest parliamentary systems. There was no king, no standing army, and no central executive. Instead, disputes were resolved through private arbitration, and enforcement was carried out by individuals and their allies. The legal system was so sophisticated that it included compensation for crimes rather than punishment, and it functioned without a monopolistic enforcer. As the historian Jesse Byock noted: > "The Icelandic Commonwealth was a society in which law and the administration of justice were in private hands, and it was the most peaceful and prospeous period in Icelandic history."

Somalia: A Stateless Society in the Modern Era

After the collapse of its central government in 1991, Somalia became a de facto stateless society. Contrary to the popular narrative of "chaos" and "anarchy" (used pejoratively), Somalia saw economic and social improvements in many areas. Private employers provided security, law, and even currency. The Somaliland region, which declared independence in 1991, has thrived without international recognition, maintaining relative stability, economic growth, and even democratic elections. As the economist Peter Leeson demonstrated in his research: > "Despite its statelessness, Somalia’s private sector has managed to provide law, order, and many other essential public goods, often doing so more effectively than the government did when it existed."

Private Communities and Seasteading

Even in today’s world, individuals and groups are creating voluntary, stateless communities. Private cities like Próspera in Honduras operate under their own legal systems, offering residents the choice of governance they prefer. Seasteading projects aim to create floating communities outside the jurisdiction of any state, where residents can experiment with new forms of social organization. Meanwhile, gated communities and homeowners’ associations (HOAs), while imperfect, demonstrate that people are willing to pay for private security, dispute resolution, and infrastructure—proving that the state is not necessary for these services.

V. The State as the Source of Society’s Ills

Not only is the state unnecessary, but it is the primary cause of many of the problems it claims to solve.

Artificial Scarcity and Economic Distortion

The state creates artificial scarcity through:

  • Licensing laws, which restrict entry into professions (e.g., medicine, law, cosmetology) to protect established interests.
  • Zoning regulations, which inflate housing prices and segregate communities.
  • Intellectual property monopolies, which stifle innovation and keep prices high (e.g., pharmaceutical patents that make life-saving drugs unaffordable).

These interventions do not protect consumers; they protect businesses from competition, leading to higher prices, lower quality, and reduced access to goods and services.

The Business Cycle and Monetary Destruction

The state’s central banking system is the root cause of economic booms and busts. By artificially suppressing interest rates and expanding the money supply, central banks like the Federal Reserve create malinvestments— projects that appear profitable only because of distorted price signals. When the bubble inevitably bursts, the economy crashes, and the state blames "capitalism" rather than its own interventions. Meanwhile, the inflation tax quietly erodes the savings of the poor and middle class, transferring wealth to the politically connected.

Perpetual War and Imperialism

The state is the greatest purveyor of violence in history. The U.S. government alone has:

  • Overthrown democratically elected leaders (e.g., Iran in 1953, Chile in 1973).
  • Bombed countless nations (Vietnam, Iraq, Libya, Syria, Yemen, and many others).
  • Maintained a global empire of over 800 military bases in 70+ countries.
  • Killed millions in wars of aggression, with no accountability for its leaders.

No private actor could ever inflict such destruction; only the state, with its monopoly on "legitimate" violence, can wage war with impunity.

The Erosion of Civil Liberties

The state is also the greatest violator of individual rights. Consider:

  • The War on Drugs, which has led to the imprisonment of millions for victimless crimes, disproportionately targeting racial minorities.
  • Mass surveillance, where the NSA and other agencies spy on Americans’ communications without warrants.
  • Civil asset forfeiture, where police can seize property without even charging the owner with a crime.
  • Qualified immunity, which shields government officials from lawsuits even when they violate constitutional rights.

In a stateless society, such violations would be impossible, as all interactions would be voluntary and subject to market accountability.

VI. A Vision of a Free Society

Imagine a society where:

  • Every interaction is voluntary. No one is forced to do anything against their will.

The ethical case for anarchism rests on the primacy of individual liberty and the principle of voluntary association. Any authority that claims the right to rule over others without their continuous, explicit consent is illegitimate. The U.S. federal government, like all states, violates the NAP on a massive scale by compelling obedience through the threat of violence. Even if a government is democratically elected, it does not have the moral authority to impose its will on dissenters, as voting cannot justify coercion against those who did not consent to be governed.

Anarchism proposes that all social interactions should be based on voluntary cooperation. Free individuals can form associations, contracts, and communities based on mutual benefit and shared values. This model respects human dignity and fosters genuine community, unlike the top-down dictates of the state. Historically, thinkers such as Pierre-Joseph Proudhon, Mikhail Bakunin, and Murray Rothbard have elaborated on these ideas, demonstrating that a stateless society is not a utopian dream but a realistic application of ethical principles.

Critics often claim that anarchism is unrealistic and that without a state, society would descend into chaos. However, numerous historical examples and modern analogues prove otherwise. During the Spanish Civil War (1936–1939), anarchist communities in Catalonia and Aragon organized themselves without a central government. Factories were collectivized, land was distributed among peasants, and decision-making occurred through grassroots assemblies. Despite facing external attacks, these communities maintained order, increased productivity, and provided for the needy through mutual aid networks. Similarly, the Free Territory of Ukraine (1918–1921), led by Nestor Makhno, implemented an anarchist society that successfully resisted both Bolshevik and White armies while organizing agriculture and industry through voluntary councils.

In the present day, the Zapatista autonomous municipalities in Chiapas, Mexico, have operated without formal state control since 1994, with local indigenous communities governing themselves through direct democracy and cooperative economics. Their success in improving education, healthcare, and economic well-being challenges the notion that a state is necessary for development. Even within the United States, voluntary associations such as credit unions, mutual aid societies, and worker cooperatives demonstrate the capacity for self-organization. Introduction

The Case for Anarchy: Why the United States Must Abolish Its Federal Government and Embrace a Stateless Society

Introduction

The United States was founded on a radical idea: that government derives its just powers from the consent of the governed. We will examine the philosophical, economic, and historical justifications for anarchism, demonstrate the failures of statism, and outline a practical path toward a stateless future.

I. The Moral Case Against the State: Coercion as the Foundation of Tyranny

1. The State is an Institution of Initiated Force

The most fundamental argument against the state is that it is inherently violent. As philosopher Ludwig von Mises argued, "The state is that institution which claims for itself the monopoly of the use of physical force in a given territorial area." This monopoly is not earned through consent but imposed through threat of violence.

  • Taxation is theft. The state does not "provide services" in exchange for taxes—it extracts wealth at gunpoint, often funding wars, surveillance, and bureaucratic waste while failing to deliver promised benefits.
  • Laws are coercive. Even "benign" laws (like speed limits or zoning regulations) are enforced through fines, imprisonment, or asset forfeiture—all of which are forms of legalized extortion.
  • War and policing are state-sanctioned violence. The U.S. military and police forces exist to suppress dissent, enforce property rights for the elite, and crush resistance—whether through domestic oppression (e.g., COINTELPRO, police brutality) or foreign aggression (e.g., Iraq, Afghanistan, Libya).

As Murray Rothbard wrote in The Ethics of Liberty, "The state is the greatest enemy of liberty, and the greatest threat to human survival." If we accept that no one has the right to initiate force against another, then the state—by definition—is illegitimate.

2. The State Corrupts Absolutely

History demonstrates that power corrupts, and absolute power corrupts absolutely. The U.S. federal government, despite its constitutional limits, has repeatedly expanded its authority through:

  • Judicial activism (e.g., Marbury v. Madison, Roe v. Wade, Obergefell v. Hodges)
  • Executive overreach (e.g., the Patriot Act, NSA surveillance, war powers usurpations)
  • Legislative overreach (e.g., Obamacare, the Affordable Care Act, COVID-19 lockdowns)

Even well-intentioned policies (like Social Security or Medicare) are unsustainable Ponzi schemes that redistribute wealth from the young to the old, distort markets, and create dependency. The state does not "help the poor"—it creates poverty by inflating money supply, suppressing wages, and stifling entrepreneurship.

3. Anarchy is Not Chaos—It is Voluntary Order

Contrary to the state’s propaganda, anarchy does not mean lawlessness. It means spontaneous order—a society where contracts, property rights, and dispute resolution emerge without coercion.

  • Private arbitration (e.g., private courts, insurance-based dispute resolution) would be more efficient and fair than state courts, which are slow, biased, and corrupt.
  • Voluntary defense agencies (e.g., private security firms, mutual defense pacts) would protect life and property better than monopolistic police, which are politicized and prone to abuse.
  • Free markets would eliminate artificial scarcity (e.g., drug prohibition, alcohol monopolies) and reduce crime by removing the state’s role as the primary criminal (e.g., war profiteering, corporate welfare, fraudulent bailouts).

As Friedrich Hayek argued in The Constitution of Liberty, "The great advantage of the market order is that it permits us to satisfy our needs with the help of people whom we do not know and in whom we need not trust." A stateless society would eliminate the need for trust in government and instead rely on voluntary exchange.

II. The Economic Case for Anarchy: How the State Destabilizes Prosperity

1. The State is the Greatest Economic Parasite

The federal government does not create wealth—it redistributes it. Through:

  • Inflationary monetary policy (the Federal Reserve devalues the dollar, making the rich richer and the poor poorer).
  • Corporate welfare (bailouts, subsidies, and monopolies distort markets and enrich crony capitalists).
  • Regulatory capture (agencies like the FDA, EPA, and SEC stifle innovation while protecting incumbent industries).

Example: The 2008 financial crisis was not caused by free markets but by government-backed mortgage fraud (Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac) and too-big-to-fail banks. The state’s "solution" was more bailouts and regulation, which prolonged the crisis rather than fixing it.

2. The State Suppresses Innovation and Entrepreneurship

Government intervention strangles economic freedom:

  • Patent and copyright monopolies (granted by the state) stifle competition and artificially inflate prices.
  • Licensing requirements (for doctors, lawyers, Uber drivers) create artificial scarcity and raise costs.
  • Minimum wage laws destroy jobs, particularly for young, unskilled workers, who are first fired when labor costs rise.

Example: Cuba and Venezuela—both highly regulated, state-controlled economies—suffer from chronic shortages, black markets, and mass emigration. Meanwhile, Hong Kong, Singapore, and Switzerland—low-tax, free-market economies—thrive with high living standards and innovation.

3. A Stateless Society Would Unleash True Prosperity

Without the state’s taxation, regulation, and inflation, we would see:

  • Hyper-efficient production (no rent-seeking, no bureaucratic waste).
  • Lower prices (no artificial scarcity, no monopoly pricing).
  • Rapid technological advancement (no FDA delays, no NSA spying on inventors).
  • Global free trade (no tariffs, no trade wars, no IMF austerity).

Historical Example: The Somalia of the 1990s, after the collapse of its central government, thrived in some areas with private security, free markets, and low crime—until foreign intervention (U.S. troops, UN "peacekeepers") restored state oppression.

III. The Historical Case: States Have Always Failed the People

1. The State is a Tool of the Elite

Governments do not exist to serve the people—they exist to serve power. Whether it’s kings, oligarchs, or corporate elites, the state always consolidates wealth and power in the hands of a few.

  • The American Revolution was not about liberty—it was about tax resistance against British rule. The Founders feared tyranny, yet they created a new tyranny (a centralized federal government).
  • The New Deal was not about helping the poor—it was about corporate welfare (e.g., agricultural subsidies, military-industrial complex).
  • The War on Drugs was not about health—it was about criminalizing the poor while allowing Wall Street to profit from private prisons.

Contrary to mainstream narratives, stateless societies have functioned better than states in many cases:

  • Post-Soviet Chechnya (1990s): After Russian forces withdrew, private security, free markets, and local governance emerged, leading to lower crime and economic growth—until Putin re-imposed state control.
  • Rojava (Syrian Kurdistan): A decentralized, democratic confederal system has reduced ISIS influence and empowered women—without a centralized state.
  • Historical Examples: The Iroquois Confederacy, medieval Iceland, and early European merchant guilds all operated without standing armies or bureaucracies—yet thrived.

3. The State is the Greatest Threat to Human Survival

States do not prevent war—they cause it. The 20th century was the bloodiest in history, yet it was also the age of the welfare state. The U.S. alone has killed millions in Vietnam, Iraq, Libya, and beyond—all under the pretense of "democracy" and "humanitarianism."

Anarchist mutual aid networks (like those in Spain during the 1936 Revolution) have saved lives without violence, while states have always failed in crises (e.g., Hurricane Katrina, COVID-19 lockdowns).

The state only has power because we obey. If enough people refuse to pay taxes, ignore laws, and opt out of state systems, the government collapses from within.

  • Tax strikes (e.g., Boston Tea Party, modern tax resistance movements) starve the beast.
  • Refusal to comply with unjust laws (e.g., draft dodging, civil disobedience) erodes legitimacy.
  • Alternative currencies (e.g., Bitcoin, local exchange systems) bypass the Federal Reserve.

2. Build Parallel Institutions

Instead of relying on the state, we must create voluntary alternatives:

  • Private courts (e.g., arbitration services, insurance-based dispute resolution).
  • Private security (e.g., Pinkerton, modern private defense firms).
  • Free schools and healthcare (e.g., homeschooling, direct primary care, medical tourism).
  • Decentralized energy and food systems (e.g., solar microgrids, urban farming).

3. Encourage Secession and Local Autonomy

The U.S. is already fracturing—states like Texas, Florida, and California are pushing for independence. If regions voluntarily secede, the federal government loses revenue and control.

  • The Catalonia example (2017): Despite Spanish state violence, the Catalan independence movement showed that people will resist oppression.

4. Spread Anarchist Ideas Through Education and Media

The state controls education and narrative, but alternative media (e.g., YouTube, podcasts, decentralized networks) can undermine its legitimacy.

  • Books: Anarchy, State, and Utopia (Robert Nozick), The Dispossessed (Ursula K. Le Guin), The Machinery of Freedom (David Friedman).

  • Online communities: r/Anarcho_Capitalism, r/Anarchism, decentralized forums.

Conclusion: The Time for Anarchy is Now

The United States federal government is a failing, corrupt, and inherently violent institution that enriches the powerful at the expense of the people. It does not protect us—it oppresses us. It does not create prosperity—it redistributes poverty.

A stateless, anarchist society—based on voluntary cooperation, individual liberty, and mutual aid—would liberate humanity from coercion, inflation, and war. History shows that without the state, people thrive. The only question is: How long will we tolerate this tyranny before we act?

The revolution will not be televised—it will be built, one voluntary community at a time. The choice is clear: Continue down the path of state collapse into chaos, or embrace anarchy and build a better world.

The time for freedom is now. The time for anarchy is now.

Choose anarchy. Choose freedom.
